newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: ASIAN EXOTICS - Central bank talks spur caution.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN EXOTICS - Central bank talks spur caution.

text.p: Southeast Asian currencies were on slightly firmer footing on Friday morning as the market paused from its recent frantic selling to await the outcome of an Asian central bankers meeting in Shanghai.
The one-day meeting, seen by some as the Asian G7, was expected to yield little more than warnings against currency speculation and talk of cooperation, but dealers said sentiment had turned wary.
"The market is cautious in case anything happens. I would advise customers to trim down their positions or just square up," a European bank dealer in Singapore said.

Dealers said some fears lingered about concerted intervention to counter the recent series of attacks on regional currencies, but most were unconvinced, given the lack of aggressive intervention so far.
"In general, it looks like the central banks have decided not to waste foreign exchange reserves intervening against market forces," a senior dealer at another European bank said.
"I'm a bit surprised they still think their currencies should be that strong with the general U.S. dollar strength we've seen over the last 24 months," he added.
In Thailand, the baht remained weak on continued commercial dollar demand and worries about the financial sector.
But dealers said trade was calmer than in recent days and the baht had steered clear of the low of 32.70 to the dollar it hit on Thursday.
Some Bangkok dealers said they saw strong support for the baht around the 32.30 level but they were not sure whether the central bank had intervened in the market.
"The market was quite calm this morning with only small buying. There was light commercial demand and the baht moved in a very tight band," a foreign bank dealer said.
The Singapore dollar bounced sharply back from its morning low of 1.4765 at the open, prompting talk of possible intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS).
But most dealers attributed the move to nervous profit-taking by a market that had bought the U.S. dollar up aggressively in the last two days.
"The MAS wouldn't come in at this level, especially as the Finance Minister has said market forces should determine the exchange rate," a dealer said.

Finance Minister Richard Hu told parliament on Wednesday Singapore's exchange rate was determined by market demand and it would continue to be managed on a trade-weighted basis with a medium-term perspective.
The Singapore dollar was expected to trade a 1.4700-1.4760 range for the day. It was at 1.4729/39 at 0440 GMT.
In Malaysia, selling of the ringgit subsided but the currency's upside was blocked around the 2.64 level to the dollar and dealers continued to predict more weakness.
"I don't think dollar/ringgit has seen a top yet. It should go to 2.70 eventually and the recent low of 2.6180/2.6200 should hold," a Singapore-based dealer said.
"The market is very quiet today, kind of in a squarish mode. They are probably waiting to see if any concrete measures emerge from Shanghai," said another Singapore dealer.
"The volume is extremely thin. 20-30 (million) dollars is moving dollar/ringgit by one big figure (100 points)," he added.
The Indonesian rupiah remained depressed below the 2,600 level to the dollar but dealers said activity had slowed.
"It's still a regional factor. Fund managers who are playing in Jakarta have also exposures in Thailand and the ringgit. Once they move, all those currencies are affected," one said.
Spot rupiah was at 2,610/20 at 0440 GMT compared with an opening of 2,601/09.
In the Philippines, the central bank sold dollars in the face of heavy commercial demand for the unit, helping to stem the peso's decline.
The Hong Kong dollar calmed down, but tensions lingered after forwards shot up on Thursday, sparking fears of a speculative attack on Asia's most strongly pegged currency.
Hong Kong Monetary Authority released Exchange Fund reserve figures after market close on Thursday, showing it held HK$569 billion at June 30, up 6.4 percent from December 31, 1996.
Analysts saw the move as aimed at scaring off speculators.
